imo-1963-01.title: Square twice, then check the conditions
imo-1963-01.body:
Since the left side is non-negative, $x\ge0$; and $x^2\ge1$, so $x\ge1$.

**Squaring.** Write the equation as $\sqrt{x^2-p}=x-2\sqrt{x^2-1}$. It is equivalent to
$$x^2-p=\big(x-2\sqrt{x^2-1}\big)^2\quad\text{together with}\quad x\ge 2\sqrt{x^2-1}.\tag{1}$$
Expanding: $x^2-p=5x^2-4-4x\sqrt{x^2-1}$, i.e.
$$4x\sqrt{x^2-1}=4x^2-4+p.\tag{2}$$
Squaring (2) (valid as an equivalence when $4x^2-4+p\ge0$):
$$16x^4-16x^2=16x^4+8(p-4)x^2+(p-4)^2\iff 8(2-p)x^2=(4-p)^2.$$
This needs $p<2$ (for $p=2$ the right side is $4\neq0$; for $p>2$ the signs disagree), and then, as $x>0$,
$$x=\frac{4-p}{\sqrt{8(2-p)}}.$$

**Checking the side conditions.** For this $x$,
$$x^2-1=\frac{(4-p)^2-8(2-p)}{8(2-p)}=\frac{p^2}{8(2-p)},\qquad 4x^2-4+p=\frac{p^2}{2(2-p)}+p=\frac{p(4-p)}{2(2-p)}.$$
- $4x^2-4+p\ge0$ (the right side of (2) equals $4x\sqrt{x^2-1}\ge0$) requires $p\ge0$.
- $x\ge2\sqrt{x^2-1}$ from (1) becomes $4-p\ge2|p|=2p$, i.e. $p\le\frac43$.
- $x^2\ge1$ holds, and $x^2-p\ge0$ follows from (1).

For $0\le p\le\frac43$ all steps are reversible, so $x=\frac{4-p}{\sqrt{8(2-p)}}$ is a root, and it is the only one. For $p<0$ or $p>\frac43$ there is no real root.

Checks: $p=0$ gives $x=1$ ($1+0=1$ ✓); $p=\frac43$ gives $x=\frac2{\sqrt3}$ ($0+2\cdot\frac1{\sqrt3}=\frac{2}{\sqrt3}$ ✓). ∎

imo-1963-02.title: Union of Thales spheres
imo-1963-02.body:
A point $P$ is such a vertex iff there is a point $X$ of segment $BC$ with $\angle APX=90^\circ$ (with $P\neq A$, $P\ne X$), i.e. iff $P$ lies on the sphere with diameter $AX$ for some $X\in BC$. So the locus is the union of the spheres $\Sigma_X$ with diameter $AX$, $X\in[BC]$.

**A cleaner description.** For a fixed $P$ consider
$$f(X)=\overrightarrow{PA}\cdot\overrightarrow{PX},\qquad X=B+\lambda(C-B),\ \lambda\in[0,1].$$
$f$ is an affine (linear) function of $\lambda$, and $f(X)=0$ means exactly $P\in\Sigma_X$ (for $P\ne A$). An affine function has a zero on $[0,1]$ iff its values at the endpoints satisfy $f(B)\,f(C)\le0$. Moreover
$$\overrightarrow{PA}\cdot\overrightarrow{PB}<0\iff P\text{ is inside the sphere with diameter }AB,$$
$=0$ on that sphere and $>0$ outside (by the same Thales argument). Hence:

**Answer.** Let $\Sigma_B$, $\Sigma_C$ be the spheres with diameters $AB$ and $AC$. The locus consists of all points $P\ne A$ that lie in the closed ball bounded by one of them and not in the open ball bounded by the other — the region "between" the two spheres, boundaries included (excluding $A$; points of the segment $BC$ itself only give degenerate angles). ∎

imo-1963-03.title: Complex numbers and Abel summation
imo-1963-03.body:
All interior angles equal $\frac{(n-2)\pi}{n}<\pi$, so walking around the polygon we turn by the same exterior angle $\frac{2\pi}{n}$ at every vertex. Rotating the picture, the $k$-th side is the vector $a_k\omega^k$ in the complex plane, where $\omega=e^{2\pi i/n}$. The polygon closes up, so
$$\sum_{k=1}^n a_k\omega^k=0.$$
Let $S_k=\omega+\omega^2+\dots+\omega^k=\frac{\omega(1-\omega^k)}{1-\omega}$, so $S_0=0$ and $S_n=0$. Summation by parts (with $a_k\omega^k=a_k(S_k-S_{k-1})$) gives
$$0=\sum_{k=1}^n a_k(S_k-S_{k-1})=a_nS_n+\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}(a_k-a_{k+1})S_k=\frac{\omega}{1-\omega}\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}d_k(1-\omega^k),$$
where $d_k=a_k-a_{k+1}\ge0$. Hence $\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}d_k(1-\omega^k)=0$, and taking real parts,
$$\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}d_k\Big(1-\cos\frac{2\pi k}{n}\Big)=0.$$
For $1\le k\le n-1$ we have $1-\cos\frac{2\pi k}n>0$, and $d_k\ge0$; a sum of non-negative terms is zero only if every term is zero. So $d_k=0$ for all $k$, i.e. $a_1=a_2=\dots=a_n$. ∎

imo-1963-04.title: Express everything through x₁ and x₂
imo-1963-04.body:
Use the 2nd, 3rd and 4th equations to express $x_3,x_4,x_5$:
$$x_3=yx_2-x_1,\qquad x_4=yx_3-x_2=(y^2-1)x_2-yx_1,$$
$$x_5=yx_4-x_3=(y^3-2y)x_2+(1-y^2)x_1.$$
The system is equivalent to these three formulas plus the 1st and 5th equations. Substituting and factoring (note $y^3-2y+1=(y-1)(y^2+y-1)$ and $y^4-3y^2+1=(y^2+y-1)(y^2-y-1)$):
$$\text{(1st)}\quad x_5+x_2-yx_1=(y^2+y-1)\big[(y-1)x_2-x_1\big]=0,$$
$$\text{(5th)}\quad x_4+x_1-yx_5=(y^2+y-1)\big[(y-1)x_1-(y^2-y-1)x_2\big]=0.$$

**Case $y^2+y-1=0$**, i.e. $y=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt5}{2}$. Both conditions hold for all $x_1,x_2$. Using $y^2=1-y$ and $y^3=2y-1$: $x_4=-yx_2-yx_1$ and $x_5=-x_2+yx_1$. So the solutions are
$$(x_1,\ x_2,\ yx_2-x_1,\ -y(x_1+x_2),\ yx_1-x_2),\qquad x_1,x_2\ \text{arbitrary}.$$

**Case $y^2+y-1\ne0$.** Then $x_1=(y-1)x_2$ and $(y-1)x_1=(y^2-y-1)x_2$, so $(y-1)^2x_2=(y^2-y-1)x_2$, i.e. $(2-y)x_2=0$.
- If $y\ne2$: $x_2=0$, so $x_1=0$ and then all $x_i=0$.
- If $y=2$: $x_1=x_2=:t$ and the formulas give $x_3=x_4=x_5=t$. All five equal (any $t$); indeed $t+t=2t$.

**Answer:** as stated above. ∎

imo-1963-04.title: Eigenvalues of the cyclic system
imo-1963-04.body: The system says $x_{k-1}+x_{k+1}=yx_k$ (indices mod $5$), i.e. $y$ is an eigenvalue of the circulant matrix with eigenvectors $v_j=(\zeta^{jk})_k$, $\zeta=e^{2\pi i/5}$, and eigenvalues $\zeta^j+\zeta^{-j}=2\cos\frac{2\pi j}{5}$: namely $2$ ($j=0$), $2\cos72^\circ=\frac{\sqrt5-1}{2}$ ($j=1,4$) and $2\cos144^\circ=-\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}$ ($j=2,3$). Nonzero solutions exist exactly for these $y$; the eigenspace is $1$-dimensional for $y=2$ (constant vectors) and $2$-dimensional for the roots of $y^2+y-1=0$, matching the first solution.

imo-1963-05.title: Telescoping with 2 sin θ
imo-1963-05.body:
Let $\theta=\frac\pi7$. Since $\cos(\pi-2\theta)=-\cos2\theta$ and $\pi-2\theta=5\theta$, the left side is
$$L=\cos\theta+\cos3\theta+\cos5\theta.$$
Multiply by $2\sin\theta\ne0$ and use $2\sin\theta\cos k\theta=\sin(k+1)\theta-\sin(k-1)\theta$:
$$2\sin\theta\,L=\sin2\theta+(\sin4\theta-\sin2\theta)+(\sin6\theta-\sin4\theta)=\sin6\theta.$$
But $\sin6\theta=\sin(\pi-\theta)=\sin\theta$. Hence $L=\frac{\sin\theta}{2\sin\theta}=\frac12$. ∎

imo-1963-05.title: Roots of unity
imo-1963-05.body:
Let $z=e^{i\pi/7}$, so $z^7=-1$ and $L=\operatorname{Re}(z+z^3+z^5)$. Now
$$z+z^3+z^5=\frac{z(1-z^6)}{1-z^2}=\frac{z-z^7}{1-z^2}=\frac{z+1}{1-z^2}=\frac{1}{1-z}.$$
For $|z|=1$, $\operatorname{Re}\frac{1}{1-z}=\frac12$ (as $\frac1{1-z}+\frac1{1-\bar z}=\frac{2-z-\bar z}{|1-z|^2}=1$). So $L=\frac12$. ∎

imo-1963-06.title: Case analysis on the two pairs
imo-1963-06.body:
The consecutive pairs of the second prediction $DAECB$ are $DA$, $AE$, $EC$, $CB$. Two *disjoint* ones must occur in the actual order: $\{DA,EC\}$, $\{DA,CB\}$ or $\{AE,CB\}$. In each case the actual order is an arrangement of two blocks and one single letter; the arrangement $DAECB$ itself is excluded (it has five, not two, correct places).

**$\{DA,EC\}$** (blocks $DA$, $EC$, letter $B$): $DABEC$, $ECDAB$, $ECBDA$, $BDAEC$, $BECDA$. Compared with $DAECB$ they have $2,1,0,0,0$ correct places; only $DABEC$ survives, but it contains $AB$, consecutive in the first prediction. ✗

**$\{AE,CB\}$** (blocks $AE$, $CB$, letter $D$): $DCBAE$, $AEDCB$, $AECBD$, $CBDAE$, $CBAED$ have $1,2,1,0,0$ correct places; only $AEDCB$ survives, but $A$ is first, as in the first prediction. ✗

**$\{DA,CB\}$** (blocks $DA$, $CB$, letter $E$): $DACBE$, $CBDAE$, $CBEDA$, $EDACB$, $ECBDA$ have $2,0,1,2,0$ correct places. $DACBE$ has $C$ third, as in the first prediction. ✗ That leaves $EDACB$.

**Check $EDACB$.** First prediction $ABCDE$: positions $E,D,A,C,B$ vs $A,B,C,D,E$ — no match; its consecutive pairs $ED,DA,AC,CB$ include none of $AB,BC,CD,DE$. Second prediction $DAECB$: $C$ and $B$ are in the predicted places (exactly two), and $DA$, $CB$ are two disjoint predicted pairs that occur. ✓

**Answer: $EDACB$.**
